references.authors: Coyle EF, Martin WH 3rd, Sinacore DR, et al.
references.title: Time course of loss of adaptations after stopping prolonged intense endurance training
references.journal: J Appl Physiol Respir Environ Exerc Physiol
references.finding: After stopping long-term endurance training, VO2max fell 7% in 21 days and stabilised 16% below trained values by 56 days; muscle oxidative enzymes fell with a half-time of ~12 days but stayed 50% above sedentary levels and capillaries did not regress over 84 days.

references.authors: Mujika I, Padilla S
references.title: Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus
references.finding: Review of short-term detraining (<4 weeks): VO2max and blood volume fall quickly in athletes, insulin sensitivity, GLUT4 and oxidative enzymes decline, while strength declines are limited.

references.authors: Mujika I, Padilla S
references.title: Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part II: Long term insufficient training stimulus
references.finding: Review of long-term detraining (>4 weeks): recently acquired VO2max gains are completely lost, whereas long-trained athletes stay above untrained values; reduced training that keeps intensity can prevent most losses.

references.authors: Hickson RC, Rosenkoetter MA
references.title: Reduced training frequencies and maintenance of increased aerobic power
references.finding: After 10 weeks of 6 days/week training raised VO2max 20-25%, cutting to 2 or 4 days/week at the same intensity maintained VO2max for a further 15 weeks.

references.authors: Hickson RC, Foster C, Pollock ML, et al.
references.title: Reduced training intensities and loss of aerobic power, endurance, and cardiac growth
references.finding: Cutting training intensity by one-third or two-thirds (frequency and duration unchanged) did not maintain VO2max or long endurance over 15 weeks; intensity is key to maintenance.

references.authors: Spiering BA, Mujika I, Sharp MA, et al.
references.title: Maintaining Physical Performance: The Minimal Dose of Exercise Needed to Preserve Endurance and Strength Over Time
references.finding: Endurance can be maintained up to 15 weeks with as few as 2 sessions/week or 33-66% less volume if intensity is kept; strength and muscle size up to 32 weeks with 1 session/week and 1 set per exercise (younger adults).

references.authors: Hawley JA, Lessard SJ
references.title: Exercise training-induced improvements in insulin action
references.finding: A single exercise bout increases muscle glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity, but the effect is short-lived and disappears after about 48 h; repeated training produces a persistent increase.

references.authors: Mikines KJ, Sonne B, Farrell PA, et al.
references.title: Effect of physical exercise on sensitivity and responsiveness to insulin in humans
references.finding: One hour of cycling raised insulin-mediated glucose uptake immediately and still 48 h later in untrained men, with glycogen synthase activity elevated for 48 h.

references.authors: Mikines KJ, Sonne B, Tronier B, et al.
references.title: Effects of acute exercise and detraining on insulin action in trained men
references.finding: In endurance-trained men, insulin sensitivity measured 15 h after the last session fell to untrained levels after 5 days without training.

references.authors: Heath GW, Gavin JR 3rd, Hinderliter JM, et al.
references.title: Effects of exercise and lack of exercise on glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity
references.journal: J Appl Physiol Respir Environ Exerc Physiol
references.finding: Ten days without exercise doubled the insulin response to a glucose load in trained people with no change in VO2max or body fat; one bout of exercise largely restored it.

references.authors: Goulet ED, Mélançon MO, Aubertin-Leheudre M, et al.
references.title: Aerobic training improves insulin sensitivity 72-120 h after the last exercise session in younger but not in older women
references.finding: Six months of training improved insulin sensitivity measured 72-120 h after the last session in younger women but not in older women, whose benefit appeared to depend on the most recent bout.

references.authors: Magkos F, Tsekouras Y, Kavouras SA, et al.
references.title: Improved insulin sensitivity after a single bout of exercise is curvilinearly related to exercise energy expenditure
references.finding: A single moderate exercise bout improved next-morning insulin sensitivity (HOMA-IR down ~32%) only when it expended more than about 900 kcal; single-bout effects last 12-48 h.

references.authors: Egan B, O'Connor PL, Zierath JR, et al.
references.title: Time course analysis reveals gene-specific transcript and protein kinetics of adaptation to short-term aerobic exercise training in human skeletal muscle
references.finding: Fourteen consecutive daily 60-min sessions raised VO2peak 17.5%; mitochondrial markers rose within the first week, while some gene transcripts rose only transiently after the first session.

references.authors: Perry CG, Lally J, Holloway GP, et al.
references.title: Repeated transient mRNA bursts precede increases in transcriptional and mitochondrial proteins during training in human skeletal muscle
references.finding: During 7 interval sessions, PGC-1alpha mRNA spiked >10-fold 4 h after each bout and returned to baseline within 24 h (saw-tooth), while PGC-1alpha protein rose after one session and plateaued at +30-40% by session 3-7; VO2peak rose 12%.

references.authors: Murias JM, Kowalchuk JM, Paterson DH
references.title: Time course and mechanisms of adaptations in cardiorespiratory fitness with endurance training in older and young men
references.finding: VO2max rose within 3 weeks of training 3x/week and kept rising to +31% (older) and +18% (young) at 12 weeks; early gains came from muscle oxygen extraction, later ones from cardiac output.

references.authors: Michailidis Y, Jamurtas AZ, Nikolaidis MG, et al.
references.title: Sampling time is crucial for measurement of aerobic exercise-induced oxidative stress
references.finding: After strenuous treadmill exercise, blood oxidative markers peaked at different times (TBARS ~1.2 h, protein carbonyls ~4.4 h, GSH/GSSG nadir ~1.7 h) and returned toward baseline within 24 h.

references.authors: Islam H, Bonafiglia JT, Turnbull PC, et al.
references.title: The impact of acute and chronic exercise on Nrf2 expression in relation to markers of mitochondrial biogenesis in human skeletal muscle
references.finding: Acute exercise raised Nrf2 and HO-1 mRNA in muscle within hours, and 4 weeks of Tabata training raised citrate synthase, Nrf2, NRF-1 and TFAM protein (HO-1 protein fell), in step with mitochondrial biogenesis.

references.authors: Morrison D, Hughes J, Della Gatta PA, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation prevents some of the cellular adaptations to endurance-training in humans
references.finding: Vitamin C plus E did not stop gains in VO2peak or mitochondrial markers over 4 weeks of interval training but prevented the training rise in SOD2.

references.authors: Tonkonogi M, Walsh B, Svensson M, et al.
references.title: Mitochondrial function and antioxidative defence in human muscle: effects of endurance training and oxidative stress
references.finding: Six weeks of endurance training raised VO2peak 24% and maximal mitochondrial respiration 40% in human muscle.

references.authors: Blair SN, Kohl HW 3rd, Barlow CE, et al.
references.title: Changes in physical fitness and all-cause mortality. A prospective study of healthy and unhealthy men
references.finding: Men who went from unfit to fit between two exams ~5 years apart had 44% lower mortality than men who stayed unfit.

references.authors: Lee DC, Sui X, Artero EG, et al.
references.title: Long-term effects of changes in cardiorespiratory fitness and body mass index on all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality in men: the Aerobics Center Longitudinal Study
references.finding: Over ~6 years, men who kept or gained fitness had 30% and 39% lower mortality than those who lost fitness; each 1-MET gain was associated with 15% lower all-cause mortality.

references.authors: Laukkanen JA, Zaccardi F, Khan H, et al.
references.title: Long-term Change in Cardiorespiratory Fitness and All-Cause Mortality: A Population-Based Follow-up Study
references.finding: Over 11 years, each 1 mL/kg/min smaller decline in measured VO2max was associated with 9% lower subsequent mortality.

references.authors: Saint-Maurice PF, Coughlan D, Kelly SP, et al.
references.title: Association of Leisure-Time Physical Activity Across the Adult Life Course With All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality
references.finding: Adults who were inactive earlier but increased activity at ages 40-61 had mortality as low as those active throughout adulthood (HR 0.65 vs 0.64).

references.authors: Kjaergaard AD, Ellervik C, Jessen N, et al.
references.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness, Body Composition, Diabetes, and Longevity: A 2-Sample Mendelian Randomization Study
references.finding: Mendelian randomization: activity, lean mass and lower body fat raise genetically predicted VO2max, but genetically predicted VO2max itself was not clearly linked to longevity, questioning causality.

references.authors: O'Donovan G, Lee IM, Hamer M, et al.
references.title: Association of "Weekend Warrior" and Other Leisure Time Physical Activity Patterns With Risks for All-Cause, Cardiovascular Disease, and Cancer Mortality
references.finding: People who packed all activity into 1-2 sessions a week (weekend warriors) had about 30% lower all-cause mortality than inactive people, similar to regularly active people.

references.authors: Dos Santos M, Ferrari G, Lee DH, et al.
references.title: Association of the "Weekend Warrior" and Other Leisure-time Physical Activity Patterns With All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality: A Nationwide Cohort Study
references.finding: For the same total weekly activity, weekend warriors had mortality similar to people active on 3 or more days.

references.authors: Montero D, Lundby C
references.title: Refuting the myth of non-response to exercise training: 'non-responders' do respond to higher dose of training
references.finding: Fitness non-response after 6 weeks fell as weekly training rose from 60 to 300 min and disappeared after a further 6 weeks with two extra sessions per week.

references.authors: Huang G, Wang R, Chen P, et al.
references.title: Dose-response relationship of cardiorespiratory fitness adaptation to controlled endurance training in sedentary older adults
references.finding: In sedentary older adults, aerobic training raised VO2max by 3.8 mL/kg/min on average; gains were largest at 66-73% of heart-rate reserve.

references.authors: Milanović Z, Sporiš G, Weston M
references.title: Effectiveness of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) and Continuous Endurance Training for VO2max Improvements: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Trials
references.finding: Endurance training raised VO2max ~4.9 and interval training ~5.5 mL/kg/min versus controls in healthy young to middle-aged adults (training periods of 2 weeks or more).

references.authors: Flockhart M, Nilsson LC, Tais S, et al.
references.title: Excessive exercise training causes mitochondrial functional impairment and decreases glucose tolerance in healthy volunteers
references.finding: Ramping training load over 4 weeks improved mitochondrial function at moderate loads, but the highest-load week sharply reduced intrinsic mitochondrial function and glucose tolerance.

references.authors: Margonis K, Fatouros IG, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
references.title: Oxidative stress biomarkers responses to physical overtraining: implications for diagnosis
references.finding: In a 12-week resistance programme, the overtraining block raised urinary isoprostanes 7-fold and protein carbonyls 73% measured 96 h after the last session, tracking the performance drop.

references.authors: Mastaloudis A, Leonard SW, Traber MG
references.title: Oxidative stress in athletes during extreme endurance exercise
references.finding: A 50 km ultramarathon raised plasma F2-isoprostanes from 75 to 131 pg/mL, which returned to baseline by 24 h after the race.

references.authors: Moritani T, deVries HA
references.title: Neural factors versus hypertrophy in the time course of muscle strength gain
references.finding: In the first 3-5 weeks of strength training, gains came mainly from neural adaptation; hypertrophy became the dominant contributor after that.

references.authors: Phillips SM, Tipton KD, Aarsland A, et al.
references.title: Mixed muscle protein synthesis and breakdown after resistance exercise in humans
references.finding: Muscle protein synthesis stayed raised 112%, 65% and 34% at 3, 24 and 48 h after one bout of resistance exercise.

references.authors: Damas F, Phillips SM, Libardi CA, et al.
references.title: Resistance training-induced changes in integrated myofibrillar protein synthesis are related to hypertrophy only after attenuation of muscle damage
references.finding: Early in resistance training, protein synthesis mostly repaired damage; it tracked hypertrophy only from about week 3 onward as damage subsided.

references.authors: Bickel CS, Cross JM, Bamman MM
references.title: Exercise dosing to retain resistance training adaptations in young and older adults
references.finding: After 16 weeks of training 3x/week, one-third or one-ninth of the dose for 32 weeks preserved hypertrophy in young but not older adults; strength was largely retained.

references.authors: Psilander N, Eftestøl E, Cumming KT, et al.
references.title: Effects of training, detraining, and retraining on strength, hypertrophy, and myonuclear number in human skeletal muscle
references.finding: After 10 weeks of one-leg training and 20 weeks off, muscle size returned to baseline but ~60% of the strength gain remained; the previously trained leg did not regrow faster.

references.authors: Cumming KT, Reitzner SM, Hanslien M, et al.
references.title: Muscle memory in humans: evidence for myonuclear permanence and long-term transcriptional regulation after strength training
references.finding: After 10 weeks of arm training and 16 weeks off, fibre size fell but extra myonuclei persisted, and retraining gave larger type 2 fibres than in the untrained arm.

references.authors: Seaborne RA, Strauss J, Cocks M, et al.
references.title: Human Skeletal Muscle Possesses an Epigenetic Memory of Hypertrophy
references.finding: DNA methylation changes from an earlier hypertrophy phase persisted through 7 weeks of unloading and were associated with greater growth on reloading.

references.authors: Ristow M, Zarse K, Oberbach A, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants prevent health-promoting effects of physical exercise in humans
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Vitamin C 1000 mg/day plus vitamin E 400 IU/day during 4 weeks of training abolished training-induced gains in insulin sensitivity and antioxidant-enzyme expression.

references.authors: Gomez-Cabrera MC, Domenech E, Romagnoli M, et al.
references.title: Oral administration of vitamin C decreases muscle mitochondrial biogenesis and hampers training-induced adaptations in endurance performance
references.finding: Vitamin C 1 g/day during 8 weeks of training hampered endurance gains and mitochondrial biogenesis markers (human and rat data).

references.authors: Paulsen G, Cumming KT, Holden G, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation hampers cellular adaptation to endurance training in humans: a double-blind, randomised, controlled trial
references.finding: Vitamin C 1000 mg plus vitamin E 235 mg daily for 11 weeks did not change VO2max gains (8% in both groups) but blunted the rise in mitochondrial proteins.

references.authors: Bjørnsen T, Salvesen S, Berntsen S, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation blunts increases in total lean body mass in elderly men after strength training
references.finding: Vitamin C 500 mg plus vitamin E 117.5 mg taken before and after each of three weekly strength sessions for 12 weeks blunted lean-mass gain (1.4% vs 3.9%).

references.authors: Yfanti C, Akerström T, Nielsen S, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant supplementation does not alter endurance training adaptation
references.finding: Vitamins C plus E during 12 weeks of strenuous cycling 5x/week did not change gains in VO2max or performance.

references.authors: Clifford T, Jeffries O, Stevenson EJ, et al.
references.title: The effects of vitamin C and E on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: a systematic review and Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Vitamin C and/or E did not significantly attenuate training gains in VO2max, endurance, lean mass or strength across trials of 4 weeks or longer.

references.authors: Roberts LJ 2nd, Oates JA, Linton MF, et al.
references.title: The relationship between dose of vitamin E and suppression of oxidative stress in humans
references.finding: With 3200 IU/day vitamin E, maximal suppression of plasma F2-isoprostanes took 16 weeks; significant falls needed 1600-3200 IU/day.

references.authors: Levine M, Conry-Cantilena C, Wang Y, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers: evidence for a recommended dietary allowance
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Plasma vitamin C saturates at about 1000 mg/day and white cells at 100 mg/day; single doses above 500 mg are poorly absorbed and the excess is excreted.

references.authors: Gonzalez DE, Dickerson BL, Roberts BM, et al.
references.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: effects of dietary antioxidants on exercise and sports performance
references.finding: ISSN position stand: supraphysiological antioxidant doses can hinder training adaptations, whole-food antioxidants are preferred, and effects depend on timing, dose and type.

references.authors: Roberts LA, Raastad T, Markworth JF, et al.
references.title: Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training
references.finding: 10 min of cold-water immersion after each session for 12 weeks blunted gains in strength and muscle mass, and reduced satellite-cell and anabolic signalling responses 24-48 h after a session.

references.authors: Fyfe JJ, Broatch JR, Trewin AJ, et al.
references.title: Cold water immersion attenuates anabolic signaling and skeletal muscle fiber hypertrophy, but not strength gain, following whole-body resistance training
references.finding: 15 min at 10 C after each session for 7 weeks attenuated type II fibre hypertrophy and post-exercise mTORC1 signalling, but not strength gains.

references.authors: Malta ES, Dutra YM, Broatch JR, et al.
references.title: The Effects of Regular Cold-Water Immersion Use on Training-Induced Changes in Strength and Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Regular post-exercise cold-water immersion impaired strength-training gains (SMD about -0.6) but did not impair endurance-training gains.

references.authors: Ihsan M, Abbiss CR, Allan R
references.title: Adaptations to Post-exercise Cold Water Immersion: Friend, Foe, or Futile?
references.finding: Review: post-exercise cold-water immersion diminishes resistance-training adaptations, while aerobic adaptations appear unaffected and may even be enhanced.

references.authors: Berjisian E, Miraftabi H, Ihsan M, et al.
references.title: Strategic Application of Post-exercise Cold-Water Immersion to Enhance Performance Recovery and Adaptation: An Umbrella Review of 15 Published Systematic Reviews with Meta-analysis
references.finding: Umbrella review: post-exercise cold-water immersion helps short-term recovery of power and jump at 24-48 h, but certainty is low to very low and adaptation effects are mode-dependent.

references.authors: Hanssen MJ, Hoeks J, Brans B, et al.
references.title: Short-term cold acclimation improves insulin sensitivity in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus
references.finding: Ten days of mild cold acclimation (14-15 C) increased peripheral insulin sensitivity by ~43%.

references.authors: Siems WG, Brenke R, Sommerburg O, et al.
references.title: Improved antioxidative protection in winter swimmers
references.finding: Winter swimmers had higher baseline erythrocyte glutathione, SOD and catalase than non-swimmers.

references.authors: Dunstan DW, Kingwell BA, Larsen R, et al.
references.title: Breaking up prolonged sitting reduces postprandial glucose and insulin responses
references.finding: Two-minute walking breaks every 20 min lowered post-drink glucose and insulin within the same day compared with uninterrupted sitting.

references.authors: Krogh-Madsen R, Thyfault JP, Broholm C, et al.
references.title: A 2-wk reduction of ambulatory activity attenuates peripheral insulin sensitivity
references.finding: Cutting steps from ~10,500 to ~1,350/day for 2 weeks lowered peripheral insulin sensitivity 17% and VO2max 7%.

references.authors: McGlory C, von Allmen MT, Stokes T, et al.
references.title: Failed Recovery of Glycemic Control and Myofibrillar Protein Synthesis With 2 wk of Physical Inactivity in Overweight, Prediabetic Older Adults
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.finding: In prediabetic older adults, 2 weeks of <1,000 steps/day worsened glycaemic control and muscle protein synthesis, which had not recovered after 2 weeks of normal activity.

references.authors: Dirks ML, Miotto PM, Goossens GH, et al.
references.title: Short-term bed rest-induced insulin resistance cannot be explained by increased mitochondrial H(2) O(2) emission
references.finding: Short-term bed rest cut insulin-stimulated glucose disposal by 42% without raising mitochondrial H2O2 emission or oxidative-stress markers.

references.authors: Kang J, Fardman BM, Ratamess NA, et al.
references.title: Efficacy of Postprandial Exercise in Mitigating Glycemic Responses in Overweight Individuals and Individuals with Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Post-meal exercise lowered glucose AUC and 24-h mean glucose (g about -0.3); bouts over 30 min did more, and starting later than 1 h after the meal may help further.

references.authors: Reynolds AN, Mann JI, Williams S, et al.
references.title: Advice to walk after meals is more effective for lowering postprandial glycaemia in type 2 diabetes mellitus than advice that does not specify timing: a randomised crossover study
references.finding: 10 min of walking after each meal lowered post-meal glucose 12% more than one daily 30-min walk, over 2-week periods.

references.authors: Francois ME, Baldi JC, Manning PJ, et al.
references.title: 'Exercise snacks' before meals: a novel strategy to improve glycaemic control in individuals with insulin resistance
references.finding: Six 1-min intense intervals before meals lowered next-24-h mean glucose more than 30 min of continuous walking.

references.authors: Little JP, Langley J, Lee M, et al.
references.title: Sprint exercise snacks: a novel approach to increase aerobic fitness
references.finding: Three 20-s sprints spread through the day, 18 sessions over 6 weeks, raised VO2peak about as much as the same sprints done together.

references.authors: Jenkins EM, Nairn LN, Skelly LE, et al.
references.title: Do stair climbing exercise "snacks" improve cardiorespiratory fitness?
references.finding: Climbing 60 stairs 3 times a day, 3 days/week for 6 weeks modestly raised VO2peak.

references.authors: Stamatakis E, Ahmadi MN, Gill JMR, et al.
references.title: Association of wearable device-measured vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity with mortality
references.finding: Three 1-2 min bursts of vigorous everyday activity a day were associated with 38-40% lower all-cause mortality over ~7 years.

references.authors: Halberg N, Henriksen M, Söderhamn N, et al.
references.title: Effect of intermittent fasting and refeeding on insulin action in healthy men
references.finding: Every-other-day 20-h fasts for 15 days raised insulin-mediated glucose uptake without weight loss; beta-hydroxybutyrate was only 0.10 mmol/L after a 20-h fast.

references.authors: Anton SD, Moehl K, Donahoo WT, et al.
references.title: Flipping the Metabolic Switch: Understanding and Applying the Health Benefits of Fasting
references.finding: The metabolic switch from glucose to fat and ketones typically occurs beyond about 12 h without food, once liver glycogen is depleted.

references.authors: Stekovic S, Hofer SJ, Tripolt N, et al.
references.title: Alternate Day Fasting Improves Physiological and Molecular Markers of Aging in Healthy, Non-obese Humans
references.finding: Four weeks of strict 36-h/12-h alternate-day fasting cut intake 37%, reduced trunk fat and raised beta-hydroxybutyrate even on eating days; no adverse effects after >6 months.

references.authors: Trepanowski JF, Kroeger CM, Barnosky A, et al.
references.title: Effect of Alternate-Day Fasting on Weight Loss, Weight Maintenance, and Cardioprotection Among Metabolically Healthy Obese Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.finding: Alternate-day fasting and daily 25% restriction lost the same weight at 6 months (-6.8% each) and 12 months (-6.0% vs -5.3%) with no differences in cardiometabolic markers.

references.authors: Harvie MN, Pegington M, Mattson MP, et al.
references.title: The effects of intermittent or continuous energy restriction on weight loss and metabolic disease risk markers: a randomized trial in young overweight women
references.finding: Over 6 months, 2 low-calorie days/week and continuous 25% restriction gave similar weight loss.

references.authors: Sundfør TM, Svendsen M, Tonstad S
references.title: Effect of intermittent versus continuous energy restriction on weight loss, maintenance and cardiometabolic risk: A randomized 1-year trial
references.finding: Intermittent (2 days/week) and continuous restriction gave similar weight loss over 6 months and similar maintenance over the next 6 months.

references.authors: Sutton EF, Beyl R, Early KS, et al.
references.title: Early Time-Restricted Feeding Improves Insulin Sensitivity, Blood Pressure, and Oxidative Stress Even without Weight Loss in Men with Prediabetes
references.finding: Five weeks of 6-h early time-restricted feeding at constant weight improved insulin sensitivity, blood pressure and oxidative stress (8-isoprostane) versus a 12-h window.

references.authors: Jamshed H, Beyl RA, Della Manna DL, et al.
references.title: Early Time-Restricted Feeding Improves 24-Hour Glucose Levels and Affects Markers of the Circadian Clock, Aging, and Autophagy in Humans
references.finding: Four days of eating 8 am-2 pm lowered 24-h glucose and raised morning ketones and expression of SIRT1 and the autophagy gene LC3A versus 8 am-8 pm.

references.authors: Liu D, Huang Y, Huang C, et al.
references.title: Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss
references.finding: With equal calorie targets, adding an 8-h eating window did not change 12-month weight loss (-8.0 vs -6.3 kg; not significant) or metabolic markers.

references.authors: Peters B, Schwarz J, Schuppelius B, et al.
references.title: Intended isocaloric time-restricted eating shifts circadian clocks but does not improve cardiometabolic health in women with overweight
references.finding: Two weeks of intended-isocaloric early or late 8-h eating shifted circadian clocks but did not improve insulin sensitivity or oxidative-stress markers.

references.authors: Cienfuegos S, Gabel K, Kalam F, et al.
references.title: Effects of 4- and 6-h Time-Restricted Feeding on Weight and Cardiometabolic Health: A Randomized Controlled Trial in Adults with Obesity
references.finding: Eight weeks of 4-h or 6-h eating windows cut intake ~550 kcal/day and weight ~3% and lowered oxidative stress versus controls.

references.authors: Wei M, Brandhorst S, Shelehchi M, et al.
references.title: Fasting-mimicking diet and markers/risk factors for aging, diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Three monthly 5-day fasting-mimicking cycles lowered weight, trunk fat, blood pressure and IGF-1; in follow-up about 3 months after the last cycle, effects on weight, IGF-1 and blood pressure had persisted (full text).

references.authors: Pietzner M, Uluvar B, Kolnes KJ, et al.
references.title: Systemic proteome adaptions to 7-day complete caloric restriction in humans
references.finding: During a 7-day water-only fast, systemic plasma proteome changes appeared only after about 3 days; weight fell 5.7 kg.

references.authors: Wilhelmi de Toledo F, Grundler F, Bergouignan A, et al.
references.title: Safety, health improvement and well-being during a 4 to 21-day fasting period in an observational study including 1422 subjects
references.finding: Buchinger fasts of 4-21 days (200-250 kcal/day) lowered weight, waist and blood pressure and raised ketones; uncontrolled observational data.

references.authors: Vendelbo MH, Clasen BF, Treebak JT, et al.
references.title: Insulin resistance after a 72-h fast is associated with impaired AS160 phosphorylation and accumulation of lipid and glycogen in human skeletal muscle
references.finding: A 72-h fast profoundly reduced muscle insulin sensitivity compared with an overnight fast.

references.authors: Dethlefsen MM, Bertholdt L, Gudiksen A, et al.
references.title: Training state and skeletal muscle autophagy in response to 36 h of fasting
references.finding: A 36-h fast changed muscle autophagy markers only modestly and only in untrained men.

references.authors: Il'yasova D, Fontana L, Bhapkar M, et al.
references.title: Effects of 2 years of caloric restriction on oxidative status assessed by urinary F2-isoprostanes: The CALERIE 2 randomized clinical trial
references.finding: CALERIE: prescribed 25% calorie restriction lowered urinary F2-isoprostanes at 12 months, and the reduction was maintained at 24 months.

references.authors: Heilbronn LK, de Jonge L, Frisard MI, et al.
references.title: Effect of 6-month calorie restriction on biomarkers of longevity, metabolic adaptation, and oxidative stress in overweight individuals: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Six months of calorie restriction lowered fasting insulin and DNA damage; protein carbonyls were unchanged.

references.authors: Marlatt KL, Redman LM, Burton JH, et al.
references.title: Persistence of weight loss and acquired behaviors 2 y after stopping a 2-y calorie restriction intervention
references.finding: Two years after the 2-year CALERIE restriction ended, participants had regained 54% of the 9 kg lost, but weight and fat stayed below baseline and controls.

references.authors: Anderson JW, Konz EC, Frederich RC, et al.
references.title: Long-term weight-loss maintenance: a meta-analysis of US studies
references.finding: Five years after structured weight-loss programmes, people maintained on average only 17-29% of the weight they had lost.

references.authors: Allaf M, Elghazaly H, Mohamed OG, et al.
references.title: Intermittent fasting for the prevention of cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Cochrane: intermittent fasting beat ad libitum eating for short-term weight loss but did not differ meaningfully from continuous energy restriction.

references.authors: Burke LM, Whitfield J, Heikura IA, et al.
references.title: Adaptation to a low carbohydrate high fat diet is rapid but impairs endurance exercise metabolism and performance despite enhanced glycogen availability
references.finding: Five to six days of a ketogenic diet raised exercise fat oxidation as much as 3-4 weeks or >12 months of adaptation, and the changes washed out in a similar 5-6 days.

references.authors: Burén J, Ericsson M, Damasceno NRT, et al.
references.title: A Ketogenic Low-Carbohydrate High-Fat Diet Increases LDL Cholesterol in Healthy, Young, Normal-Weight Women: A Randomized Controlled Feeding Trial

timing.summary: Each session gives a burst of redox signalling and better glucose handling that lasts one to two days, while repeated sessions build fitness, mitochondria and antioxidant defences over weeks and the survival benefit tracks fitness kept up over years. Recently gained fitness fades within one to two months of stopping, so the habit matters more than any single block of training.

onset.text: Within hours: blood oxidative markers peak 1-4 h after hard exercise and settle within 24 h [tbody-michailidis2007]; PGC-1alpha and Nrf2 signals spike after each bout [tbody-perry2010, tbody-islam2020]; insulin sensitivity is raised the same day [tbody-mikines1988]. Muscle mitochondrial markers rise within the first week [tbody-egan2013].

full.text: VO2max rises within 3 weeks and was still climbing at 12 weeks (+18% young, +31% older men) [tbody-murias2010]; gains keep growing with more weekly dose [tbody-montero2017]. Mortality benefit accrues over years: men who went from unfit to fit over ~5 years had 44% lower mortality than those who stayed unfit [tbody-blair1995].

after_stopping.text: The single-bout insulin effect is gone after about 2-5 days [tbody-hawley2008, tbody-mikines1989]. Recently gained VO2max is completely lost after more than 4 weeks off [tbody-mujika2000b]; in long-trained people VO2max fell 7% in 3 weeks and settled 16% lower by 8 weeks, and muscle oxidative enzymes halved in ~12 days but stayed above sedentary levels [tbody-coyle1984].

frequency.text: Because one session's insulin-sensitising effect lasts roughly 48 h [tbody-hawley2008, tbody-mikines1988], exercising at least every second day keeps it continuous. Building fitness needs more than keeping it: after 10 weeks of training, 2 sessions a week at the same intensity maintained VO2max for 15 weeks [tbody-hickson1981, tbody-spiering2021], whereas lowering intensity did not [tbody-hickson1985].

sperm.late_start: Starting 2-4 weeks before still improves insulin sensitivity and fitness quickly, but only reaches sperm in their last maturation steps; no trial shows semen changes that fast.
sperm.text: New sperm take about 64 days (42-76) to reach the ejaculate [tbody-misell2006], so a new programme needs 2-3 months to show in semen; the trial that improved semen in obese men ran 16 weeks [tbody-rosety2017]. Evidence is mostly observational [tbody-gaskins2015].

egg.late_start: Insulin sensitivity improves within days of starting, which may help the final follicle phase, but there is no direct trial evidence for a late start.
egg.text: The ovulatory follicle grows for about 85 days before ovulation [tbody-gougeon1986]; exercise likely acts through insulin sensitivity and weight, which change over weeks to months. Intervention trials in women with reproductive problems are few and small [tbody-mena2019].

timing.debate: Fitness gains are linked to lower mortality in cohorts [tbody-blair1995, tbody-lee2011], and starting in midlife looked as good as lifelong activity [tbody-saintmaurice2019], but Mendelian randomization questions whether fitness itself causes longevity [tbody-kjaergaard2025]. On frequency, the short-lived insulin effect argues for frequent sessions [tbody-hawley2008], yet people who do all their activity on 1-2 days have similar mortality to regular exercisers [tbody-odonovan2017, tbody-dossantos2022].

timing.summary: Fasting days start changing insulin action within about two weeks, but the main effect, weight loss, builds over about six months and then levels off. When fasting stops, the gains last only as long as the lost weight stays off.

onset.text: Insulin-mediated glucose uptake improved after 15 days of every-other-day 20-h fasts even without weight loss [tbody-halberg2005]; a 20-h fast raises ketones only slightly (0.10 mmol/L), whereas strict 36-h fasts raised BHB even on eating days after 4 weeks [tbody-stekovic2019].

full.text: Weight loss reached about -6.8% at 6 months and was -6.0% at 12 months, the same as daily 25% restriction [tbody-trepanowski2017].

after_stopping.text: Not measured specifically after stopping ADF. In general, 4-5 years after structured weight-loss programmes people kept only 17-29% of the weight they had lost [tbody-anderson2001], and weight-related benefits fade with regain.

frequency.text: The schedule itself (fast every other day) adds nothing measurable over the same calorie deficit spread daily: weight, insulin and CRP matched daily restriction at 6 and 12 months [tbody-trepanowski2017, tbody-allaf2021]. Pick whichever pattern can be sustained.

timing.debate: A strict 36-h ADF trial reported improved ageing markers and ketones on eating days [tbody-stekovic2019], but a year-long trial found no advantage over daily restriction, with more dropouts [tbody-trepanowski2017], and Cochrane found no meaningful difference from continuous restriction [tbody-allaf2021].

timing.summary: High-dose vitamin C and E start blunting training signals within weeks, because they flatten the exercise ROS pulse that triggers adaptation, and the blunting of mitochondrial and muscle gains shows up over 1-3 months. Vitamin C saturates the blood within days, while vitamin E builds slowly over months.

onset.text: Four weeks of 1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E during training abolished the gain in insulin sensitivity and antioxidant-enzyme expression [tbody-ristow2009]; plasma vitamin C saturates at ~1000 mg/day [tbody-levine1996].

full.text: Blunted mitochondrial proteins after 11 weeks [tbody-paulsen2014] and smaller lean-mass gain after 12 weeks [tbody-bjornsen2016]; vitamin E took 16 weeks to reach its maximal effect on F2-isoprostanes [tbody-roberts2007].

after_stopping.text: Not measured. Vitamin C excess is excreted within days [tbody-levine1996]; vitamin E builds and probably clears more slowly [tbody-roberts2007]. Whether blunted adaptations catch up after stopping has not been tested.

frequency.text: Blunting was seen both with daily dosing [tbody-paulsen2014] and with doses taken only around strength sessions [tbody-bjornsen2016]; no trial has compared taking the same dose far from sessions, so timing away from training is not a proven fix [tbody-gonzalez2026].

timing.debate: Trials showing blunted adaptations [tbody-ristow2009, tbody-gomezcabrera2008, tbody-paulsen2014] conflict with trials and a meta-analysis showing no loss of VO2max, endurance or strength gains [tbody-yfanti2010, tbody-clifford2020]; molecular markers are blunted more consistently than performance [tbody-morrison2015].

timing.summary: Moderate calorie restriction lowers oxidative and metabolic markers within months, reaches its full effect over about a year, and holds while restriction continues. After stopping, about half the lost weight returned within two years, but people were still lighter than at the start.

onset.text: The earliest measured point in the long trials was 6 months, when fasting insulin and DNA damage were already lower [tbody-heilbronn2006]; earlier time points were not measured for oxidative markers.

full.text: Urinary F2-isoprostanes were lower at 12 months and the reduction held at 24 months of ~12-15% achieved restriction [tbody-ilyasova2018].

after_stopping.text: Two years after CALERIE ended, participants had regained 54% of the 9 kg they lost, yet weight and fat mass stayed below baseline and below controls [tbody-marlatt2017]. Whether oxidative markers stayed low was not measured.

frequency.text: Studied as a continuous daily deficit; intermittent schedules give similar weight loss for the same deficit [tbody-allaf2021].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; the main uncertainty is whether the marker changes are due to restriction itself or simply weight loss [tbody-heilbronn2006, tbody-ilyasova2018].

timing.summary: Fitness rises measurably within 2-3 weeks of training and keeps rising for months with enough dose, and the mortality benefit comes from fitness held for years. It is lost faster than it is gained: recent gains disappear within about a month off.

onset.text: VO2peak rose 17.5% after 14 daily sessions [tbody-egan2013] and VO2max was higher within 3 weeks of training three times a week [tbody-murias2010].

full.text: Still rising at 12 weeks [tbody-murias2010]; people who do not respond at low doses respond when weekly training is increased [tbody-montero2017]. Over 5-6 years, gaining or keeping fitness was associated with 30-44% lower mortality than losing it or staying unfit [tbody-blair1995, tbody-lee2011].

after_stopping.text: VO2max fell 7% within 3 weeks and 16% by 8 weeks in trained people [tbody-coyle1984]; recently acquired gains are completely lost after more than 4 weeks [tbody-mujika2000b]; even 2 weeks of very low step counts cut VO2max 7% [tbody-kroghmadsen2010].

frequency.text: Two sessions a week at unchanged intensity maintained a training-induced VO2max rise for 15 weeks [tbody-hickson1981, tbody-spiering2021]; cutting intensity by a third did not [tbody-hickson1985].

timing.debate: Cohorts tie changes in fitness to mortality [tbody-lee2011, tbody-laukkanen2016], but Mendelian randomization found no clear causal effect of genetically higher VO2max on longevity [tbody-kjaergaard2025].

timing.summary: A cold plunge right after strength training dampens muscle-building signals for one to two days, and done after every session for 7-12 weeks it leaves smaller muscle gains. Repeated cold exposure on its own can raise insulin sensitivity within about ten days, but long-term health effects are unproven.

onset.text: After one session, cold immersion reduced satellite-cell and anabolic signalling at 24-48 h [tbody-roberts2015] and mTORC1 signalling at 1 h [tbody-fyfe2019]; 10 days of mild cold acclimation raised insulin sensitivity ~43% in type 2 diabetes [tbody-hanssen2015].

full.text: Smaller gains in muscle mass after 7-12 weeks of post-session immersion [tbody-fyfe2019, tbody-roberts2015, tbody-malta2021]. Higher antioxidant enzymes in seasoned winter swimmers come from cross-sectional data [tbody-siems1999].

after_stopping.text: Not measured; whether blunted hypertrophy is regained later was not tested.

frequency.text: Keep cold plunges away from strength sessions. No trial tested how many hours of separation is enough; the 24-48 h anabolic window [tbody-roberts2015] suggests separating by at least several hours or using cold on non-lifting days (extrapolated). Endurance adaptations were not harmed [tbody-malta2021].

timing.debate: For endurance training, some argue post-exercise cooling may even enhance mitochondrial adaptation [tbody-ihsan2021], while an umbrella review rates the certainty of all cold-water findings as low to very low [tbody-berjisian2026].

timing.summary: Any effect of heavy cycling on sperm would act on sperm still developing in the testis, so changes would show and fade on the timescale of sperm production, about two to three months. No study has measured this time course directly.

onset.text: Not measured; the association is cross-sectional (5+ h/week linked to low sperm concentration) [tbody-wise2011].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured in cyclists. Extrapolated from sperm production: newly made sperm reach the ejaculate after ~64 days (42-76) [tbody-misell2006], so allow about 3 months after cutting back.

frequency.text: The association appears only above about 5 h/week [tbody-wise2011]; moderate cycling is not a concern, and overall activity was linked to better semen [tbody-gaskins2015].

sperm.late_start: Cutting back 2-4 weeks before only spares the final maturation of sperm already formed; the benefit, if any, is unknown.
sperm.text: Heat or saddle pressure would act on developing sperm; the ~64-day production time [tbody-misell2006] sets a 2-3 month lead time (extrapolated).

timing.debate: One fertility-clinic cohort linked 5+ h/week of cycling to low sperm concentration [tbody-wise2011], while young men with more overall activity had better counts [tbody-gaskins2015]. A cycling-training trial from an author group with several retracted exercise-semen trials was deliberately not used.

timing.summary: Evening light suppresses melatonin within minutes to hours and shifts the body clock later over a few evenings; one night of sleeping with the light on worsened next-morning insulin resistance. These effects reverse within days once evenings are kept dim and days bright.

onset.text: Room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99% of people and shortened melatonin by ~90 min the same night [tbody-gooley2011]; one night at 100 lux during sleep raised next-morning insulin resistance [tbody-mason2022].

full.text: Five evenings of e-reader use delayed the circadian clock and lengthened sleep onset [tbody-chang2015].

after_stopping.text: Natural light re-anchored the clock within a weekend (about 69% of a week's shift) and fully within a week [tbody-stothard2017, tbody-wright2013].

frequency.text: Effects act night by night, so dim evenings need to be a nightly habit; a single bright evening resets only partially within days.

timing.debate: Laboratory effects within days are clear [tbody-chang2015], but a published letter argued that these lab findings may not reflect real-life exposure [tbody-zeitzer2015].

timing.summary: Short vigorous bursts lower that day's blood sugar, and done several times a day for six weeks they modestly raise fitness. Like other exercise, the effect needs repeating to persist.

onset.text: Six 1-min intense intervals before meals lowered the next 24 h of glucose [tbody-francois2014].

full.text: VO2peak rose after 6 weeks of 3 daily stair-climb or sprint snacks [tbody-jenkins2019, tbody-little2019]; longer trials are lacking.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; by analogy with other training, gains would fade within weeks [tbody-mujika2000b] (extrapolated).

frequency.text: Sprints spread across the day raised fitness about as much as the same sprints done in one session [tbody-little2019]; the glucose effect is per meal, so snacks before or after main meals are the logical timing [tbody-francois2014].

timing.debate: Cohort data link three 1-2 min daily bursts to 38-40% lower mortality [tbody-stamatakis2022], far more than the modest fitness gains seen in 6-week trials [tbody-jenkins2019] would predict.

timing.summary: A ketone ester drink raises blood ketones within an hour and they are back to baseline within a few hours; nothing builds up with daily use. Any glucose benefit lasts only as long as the dosing continues.

onset.text: Peak ketones within 1-2 h of a monoester dose [tbody-clarke2012].

full.text: No cumulative build-up: three drinks a day for 28 days gave the same post-drink rises without changes in weight, glucose or lipids [tbody-sotomota2019]; pre-meal dosing for 14 days lowered 24-h glucose [tbody-walsh2021].

after_stopping.text: Ketones fall back within a few hours of each dose (half-life roughly 1-3 h) [tbody-clarke2012].

frequency.text: Effects last hours, so they need dosing before each meal to matter for glucose [tbody-walsh2021]; there is no evidence for intermittent schedules.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

timing.summary: Three monthly five-day cycles lowered weight, IGF-1 and blood pressure, and in a voluntary follow-up these changes had largely persisted about three months after the last cycle. This rests on one company-linked trial with no control during follow-up.

onset.text: Changes were measured only after three monthly cycles, 5-7 days after returning to normal eating [tbody-wei2017].

full.text: Measured after 3 cycles (3 months) [tbody-wei2017]; whether more cycles add more is unknown.

after_stopping.text: Effects on weight, waist, IGF-1 and blood pressure persisted for about 3 months (mean 3.2) after the final cycle in the 50 people followed up [tbody-wei2017].

frequency.text: Tested as 5 days per month for 3 months [tbody-wei2017]; no trial compared other spacing.

timing.debate: The trial authors note that lifestyle changes during follow-up may explain the persistence, and the lead developer holds a commercial interest in the diet [tbody-wei2017]; intermittent schemes generally match simple calorie restriction [tbody-allaf2021].

timing.summary: Two low-calorie days a week produce weight loss that builds for about six months, matching continuous dieting. The benefits last only as long as the weight stays off.

onset.text: Not reported at early time points in the trials reviewed; weight loss was measured at 6 months [tbody-harvie2011].

full.text: Weight loss similar to continuous restriction at 6 months, then held over a further 6-month maintenance phase [tbody-harvie2011, tbody-sundfor2018].

after_stopping.text: Not measured for 5:2 specifically; after structured diets people keep only 17-29% of lost weight at 4-5 years [tbody-anderson2001].

frequency.text: Two fasting days a week; no advantage over the same deficit spread daily [tbody-sundfor2018, tbody-allaf2021].

timing.debate: Fasting-specific benefits are proposed via the metabolic switch [tbody-anton2018], but trials matched for calories show no difference from continuous restriction [tbody-allaf2021, tbody-sundfor2018].

timing.summary: Glucose spikes raise oxidative stress within an hour or two, HbA1c takes about three months to show a change, and glycation of long-lived proteins accumulates over years. Good control early has a 'legacy' effect that protected against heart attacks and death for up to 24 years after the trials ended.

onset.text: A glucose load doubled leukocyte ROS at 2 h [tbody-mohanty2000]; after glucose was normalised, fasting glucose fell with a half-time of ~6 days and fructosamine ~12 days [tbody-tahara1995].

full.text: HbA1c fell with a half-time of ~35 days, so a new steady state takes about 3 months [tbody-tahara1995]; skin collagen glycation was 30% lower after ~5 years of intensive control [tbody-monnier1999], reflecting years-long collagen turnover [tbody-verzijl2000].

after_stopping.text: HbA1c differences vanished within a year after UKPDS, yet lower microvascular risk persisted and lower heart attacks and death emerged [tbody-holman2008], with no sign of waning at 24 years [tbody-adler2024]; DCCT intensive therapy cut cardiovascular events 42% over 17 years [tbody-nathan2005].

frequency.text: Glucose excursions act meal by meal and day by day [tbody-mohanty2000, tbody-ceriello2008], so control has to be continuous; the long glycation turnover means earlier is better.

egg.late_start: Lowering glucose in the last weeks still helps the periovulatory egg and early embryo, but HbA1c and birth-defect risk reflect the preceding ~3 months.
egg.text: Birth-defect risk rose with HbA1c measured within 3 months around conception [tbody-ludvigsson2018]; HbA1c needs ~3 months to settle [tbody-tahara1995] and the ovulatory follicle grows for ~85 days [tbody-gougeon1986]. Diabetes is linked to lower fecundability [tbody-whitworth2011].

sperm.late_start: Unknown; only the final maturation stage would be covered.
sperm.text: Extrapolated from the ~64-day sperm production time [tbody-misell2006]; direct timing data in men are lacking.

timing.debate: Glucose swings, more than HbA1c, tracked oxidative stress in type 2 diabetes [tbody-monnier2006] and in clamp studies [tbody-ceriello2008], but in type 1 diabetes glucose variability was not associated with urinary isoprostanes [tbody-wentholt2008].

timing.summary: There is no credible measured effect on oxidative stress, so there is no time course to describe. Claims come from small proponent studies.

onset.text: Not measured in credible controlled studies [tbody-chevalier2012].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: No evidence-based schedule.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

timing.summary: Interval sessions trigger mitochondrial signalling after the first bout and raise fitness within two weeks, with gains building over months. Fitness built this way needs intensity kept up to be maintained, and too much hard work too fast damages mitochondria.

onset.text: PGC-1alpha protein rose after one session and plateaued after 3-7 sessions, with VO2peak +12% after 7 interval sessions in 2 weeks [tbody-perry2010].

full.text: Across trials of 2 weeks or more, interval training raised VO2max ~5.5 mL/kg/min versus ~4.9 for continuous training [tbody-milanovic2015]; a long-term plateau is not well defined.

after_stopping.text: Same detraining as other aerobic training: recent gains are lost after more than 4 weeks [tbody-mujika2000b]; VO2max fell 7% in 3 weeks in trained people [tbody-coyle1984].

frequency.text: 2-3 hard sessions a week; maintaining fitness needs intensity kept [tbody-hickson1985]. Ramping load too quickly impaired mitochondrial function and glucose tolerance within the peak week [tbody-flockhart2021].

sperm.late_start: Unknown; only late maturation stages are covered.
sperm.text: Extrapolated from the ~64-day sperm production time [tbody-misell2006]; no reliable trial of interval training on semen exists.

timing.debate: Intervals give more fitness per minute [tbody-milanovic2015], but rapidly escalating high-intensity load reduced mitochondrial function [tbody-flockhart2021], so more is not always better on short timescales.

timing.summary: Some glucose and insulin effects appear within days, but the main benefit is weight loss building over about six months and matching ordinary dieting. Benefits fade as weight returns.

onset.text: Four days of early time-restricted eating lowered 24-h glucose [tbody-jamshed2019]; 15 days of alternate 20-h fasts improved insulin action [tbody-halberg2005].

full.text: Weight loss plateaued by 6-12 months and matched daily restriction [tbody-trepanowski2017, tbody-liu2022].

after_stopping.text: Not measured specifically; long-term weight maintenance after any diet is poor [tbody-anderson2001].

frequency.text: Daily windows, alternate days and 2 days a week all perform about like continuous restriction [tbody-allaf2021]; choose by sustainability.

timing.debate: Early time-restricted feeding improved insulin sensitivity and oxidative stress without weight loss in 5 weeks [tbody-sutton2018], but isocaloric 8-h windows for 2 weeks [tbody-peters2025] and calorie-matched TRE over 12 months [tbody-liu2022] showed no extra benefit.

timing.summary: Ketosis starts within a day or two of cutting carbohydrate and the body's fuel use adapts within about a week, faster than often claimed; LDL can rise within three weeks. Glycaemic benefits peak around six months and shrink by a year, and the metabolic adaptation reverses within days of eating carbohydrate again.

onset.text: The switch to fat and ketones begins beyond ~12 h without carbohydrate [tbody-anton2018] (a 20-h fast gave only 0.10 mmol/L BHB [tbody-halberg2005]); exercise fat oxidation reached chronic-adapted levels after 5-6 days [tbody-burke2021].

full.text: LDL rose after 3-4 weeks in lean adults [tbody-retterstol2018, tbody-buren2021]; diabetes remission, weight and triglyceride benefits were greatest at 6 months and diminished by 12 months [tbody-goldenberg2021].

after_stopping.text: Metabolic adaptations washed out in a similar 5-6 days [tbody-burke2021].

frequency.text: Ketosis depends on continuous restriction; occasional carbohydrate meals reverse it, and adaptation is quickly lost [tbody-burke2021].

timing.debate: Benefits at 6 months diminish by 12 months as adherence falls [tbody-goldenberg2021], and LDL rises within weeks in lean people [tbody-buren2021, tbody-retterstol2018]; the common claim that 'keto-adaptation' takes many weeks is contradicted by adaptation in 5-6 days in elite athletes [tbody-burke2021].

timing.summary: Eating close to bedtime worsens that meal's glucose handling the same evening, and a few days of late eating raises hunger and lowers energy expenditure. Moving meals earlier reverses this from the next meal.

onset.text: The same glucose load 1 h rather than 4 h before habitual bedtime gave higher glucose and lower insulin [tbody-garaulet2022]; late isocaloric eating raised hunger and lowered energy expenditure within days [tbody-vujovic2022].

full.text: Acute; no build-up beyond the days studied has been shown.

after_stopping.text: Effects are tied to each meal's timing; extrapolated to reverse from the next earlier meal.

frequency.text: A nightly habit matters; occasional late meals have only same-night effects.

timing.debate: Laboratory studies show acute harm from late meals [tbody-garaulet2022, tbody-vujovic2022], but 2 weeks of early versus late 8-h eating windows at intended equal calories did not change insulin sensitivity [tbody-peters2025].

timing.summary: Lower glucose peaks start with the first meals, while HbA1c, weight and triglyceride benefits build over months, peaking around six months. They shrink by a year as adherence slips and reverse if the diet stops.

onset.text: Post-meal glucose and oxidative bursts depend on each meal's carbohydrate load [tbody-mohanty2000]; trials first measured HbA1c and weight at 3-6 months [tbody-goldenberg2021].

full.text: Largest improvements at 6 months, diminished at 12 months [tbody-goldenberg2021].

after_stopping.text: Not measured; HbA1c would drift back over about 3 months given its ~35-day half-time [tbody-tahara1995] (extrapolated).

frequency.text: Effects depend on everyday meals; LDL can rise within 3 weeks on very low intakes in lean people [tbody-retterstol2018].

timing.debate: Remission and weight benefits seen at 6 months shrank to small or trivial by 12 months [tbody-goldenberg2021]; no substantive published debate on timing beyond this was found.

timing.summary: Most trials run 8-12 weeks and show modest falls in cortisol and blood pressure; one intensive 3-day retreat was followed by lower IL-6 four months later. Direct oxidative-stress time courses are not known.

onset.text: Not well measured; most trials assess only at the end of 8-12 week programmes [tbody-pascoe2017].

full.text: Modest cortisol and blood-pressure reductions after typical 8-12 week programmes [tbody-pascoe2017].

after_stopping.text: IL-6 was lower 4 months after a 3-day intensive retreat in stressed adults [tbody-creswell2016]; otherwise not measured.

frequency.text: Trials mostly used several sessions a week; no trial compared schedules.

timing.debate: A systematic review judged immune and inflammation effects tentative and heterogeneous [tbody-black2016], while a small RCT found lasting IL-6 reductions after a brief retreat [tbody-creswell2016].

timing.summary: Metformin acts within days and clears within a day or two of stopping, but its interaction with exercise shows up over 3-4 months of training and its lowering of vitamin B12 accumulates over years. In UKPDS, early metformin use left a long-term legacy benefit.

onset.text: Half-life ~5 h with good kidney function [tbody-graham2011]; glucose effects begin within days of reaching dose (extrapolated from pharmacokinetics).

full.text: Blunted gains in insulin sensitivity, VO2max and mitochondrial respiration over 12 weeks of aerobic training [tbody-konopka2019] and in lean mass over 14 weeks of resistance training [tbody-walton2019]; B12 fell 19% over 4.3 years [tbody-dejager2010], with risk rising per year of use [tbody-aroda2016].

after_stopping.text: The drug itself clears within 1-2 days [tbody-graham2011]. In UKPDS, the cardiovascular and mortality benefit of early metformin persisted for 10-24 years after the trial [tbody-holman2008, tbody-adler2024].

frequency.text: Prescribed daily, usually split with meals. Whether separating doses from exercise sessions avoids blunting has not been tested.

timing.debate: Metformin blunted exercise adaptations in older adults [tbody-konopka2019, tbody-walton2019], yet carried a long legacy benefit in overweight people with type 2 diabetes [tbody-holman2008]; the two findings concern different populations.

timing.summary: Bright daytime and morning light moves the body clock earlier within a weekend and fully within a week, and light therapy improves sleep problems over weeks. The clock drifts later again when daylight is lost.

onset.text: A summer weekend of natural light achieved ~69% of a week's circadian advance [tbody-stothard2017].

full.text: One week of natural light aligned the clock to sunrise and sunset [tbody-wright2013]; light therapy improved sleep problems in trials lasting weeks [tbody-vanmaanen2016].

after_stopping.text: Not measured directly; the delay seen in typical weekends under electric light [tbody-stothard2017] suggests the shift reverses within days.

frequency.text: The clock is reset daily, so daily outdoor light, especially early in the day, is needed.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

timing.summary: Large calorie surpluses cause insulin resistance and oxidative stress within two to three days, before any inflammation, and moderate surpluses raise oxidative markers within a month. The damage lasts as long as the extra fat does.

onset.text: About 6000 kcal/day caused systemic insulin resistance and oxidative stress within 2-3 days [tbody-boden2015].

full.text: +1000 kcal/day for 28 days raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and muscle protein carbonyls [tbody-samochabonet2012]; with continued surplus weight keeps rising.

after_stopping.text: Not measured after overfeeding ends.

frequency.text: Even a few days of large surplus matter [tbody-boden2015].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

timing.summary: A single ultra-race doubles a lipid-peroxidation marker that returns to normal within a day, but weeks of excessive load without recovery cause sustained oxidative stress, mitochondrial impairment and performance loss. Recovery depends on reducing the load.

onset.text: F2-isoprostanes rose during a 50 km race [tbody-mastaloudis2001]; in a 4-week ramp, mitochondrial function fell in the highest-load week [tbody-flockhart2021].

full.text: A 3-week overtraining block raised urinary isoprostanes 7-fold still 96 h after the last session [tbody-margonis2007].

after_stopping.text: Single-race markers returned to baseline by 24 h [tbody-mastaloudis2001]; recovery from multi-week overreaching was not quantified in the trials reviewed.

frequency.text: Build load gradually; markers stayed high 4 days after sessions in an overtraining block [tbody-margonis2007].

sperm.text: High-mileage runners had lower testosterone and poorer semen [tbody-desouza1994]; any reversal would follow the ~64-day production time [tbody-misell2006] (extrapolated).

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; the threshold between productive overload and overreaching is individual [tbody-flockhart2021, tbody-margonis2007].

timing.summary: A walk after a meal lowers that meal's glucose rise within the hour and trims the whole day's average. The effect does not carry over much, so it works best as a daily habit after main meals.

onset.text: Lowers the glucose curve of the meal it follows [tbody-reynolds2016, tbody-kang2023].

full.text: Also lowers 24-h mean glucose [tbody-kang2023]; three 15-min walks after meals improved 24-h glycaemia [tbody-reynolds2016].

after_stopping.text: Extrapolated: single-bout effects on insulin action last at most 1-2 days [tbody-hawley2008].

frequency.text: After each main meal, especially the largest; bouts over 30 min did more [tbody-kang2023].

timing.debate: Most advice is to walk straight after eating [tbody-reynolds2016], while a meta-analysis suggested starting after the first hour may lower 24-h glucose more [tbody-kang2023].

timing.summary: Systemic changes need about three days of fasting to appear, and muscle becomes temporarily insulin resistant by day three. There are no controlled data on how long any benefit lasts after refeeding.

onset.text: Plasma proteome changes appeared only after ~3 days of water-only fasting [tbody-pietzner2024]; a 72-h fast markedly reduced muscle insulin sensitivity [tbody-vendelbo2012]; ketones rose in clinic fasts [tbody-wilhelmidetoledo2019].

full.text: Weight, waist and blood pressure fell over 5-20 day clinic fasts (uncontrolled) [tbody-wilhelmidetoledo2019].

after_stopping.text: Not measured in controlled trials.

frequency.text: No evidence-based schedule; any repeat interval is untested.

timing.debate: Autophagy is often claimed after 1-3 days, but a 36-h fast changed human muscle autophagy markers only modestly [tbody-dethlefsen2018], while blood-cell autophagy gene expression rose with early daily time-restricted eating [tbody-jamshed2019].

timing.summary: Stress episodes lasting weeks were linked to lower seminal glutathione and poorer sperm that had recovered three months later, and years of chronic stress track with oxidative damage and shorter telomeres. For egg and IVF outcomes, pre-treatment distress showed no effect.

onset.text: Not precisely measured; during an exam period seminal glutathione and sperm motility were lower than 3 months later [tbody-eskiocak2005].

full.text: Chronic stress over years was associated with higher oxidative stress and shorter telomeres (cross-sectional) [tbody-epel2004].

after_stopping.text: Sperm measures and seminal glutathione had recovered 3 months after exams [tbody-eskiocak2005], consistent with sperm production time [tbody-misell2006].

frequency.text: Stress-reduction practices are studied as regular programmes [tbody-pascoe2017].

sperm.late_start: Reducing stress late may not change sperm already formed.
sperm.text: Stress was linked to lower sperm concentration [tbody-nordkap2016] and reversed within one sperm cycle after exams [tbody-eskiocak2005].

timing.debate: Stress is associated with poorer semen [tbody-nordkap2016, tbody-eskiocak2005], but pre-treatment anxiety or depression did not predict IVF pregnancy [tbody-boivin2011].

timing.summary: Rapamycin's long half-life means blood levels build over days, and the rationale for weekly rather than daily dosing is to hit mTORC1 while sparing mTORC2 (mainly mouse data). A 6-week rapalog course was linked to fewer infections for a year, but a year of weekly rapamycin did not change its primary outcome.

onset.text: Steady-state blood levels take at least 4 days [tbody-mahalati2001]; immune effects were measured after 6 weeks of a rapalog [tbody-mannick2014].

full.text: No plateau defined; 48 weeks of 5-10 mg weekly did not change visceral fat [tbody-moel2025].

after_stopping.text: After a 6-week course of a TORC1 inhibitor combination (not rapamycin), fewer infections were reported over the year after starting [tbody-mannick2018].

frequency.text: In mice, intermittent dosing spared glucose tolerance and immunity compared with daily dosing, because chronic exposure also inhibits mTORC2 [tbody-arriolaapelo2016, tbody-lamming2012]; daily 1 mg was tolerated for 8 weeks in older humans [tbody-kraig2018]. No human trial has compared schedules.

timing.debate: The weekly-dosing rationale rests on mouse data [tbody-arriolaapelo2016], and the only year-long human trial of weekly rapamycin missed its primary outcome [tbody-moel2025].

timing.summary: A sugary load raises white-cell ROS output within one to two hours, and repeated spikes across a day do more harm than steady high glucose. Each spike passes in hours, but habitual intake shows up in HbA1c over about three months.

onset.text: 75 g glucose doubled leukocyte ROS at 2 h and lowered vitamin E within 1 h [tbody-mohanty2000].

full.text: Glucose oscillating over 24 h worsened endothelial function and oxidative stress more than constant high glucose [tbody-ceriello2008].

after_stopping.text: Each spike resolves within hours [tbody-mohanty2000]; HbA1c reflects intake over the past ~3 months [tbody-tahara1995].

frequency.text: Effects are per meal or drink; fewer and smaller spikes matter more than occasional treats.

sperm.text: Men drinking 1.3+ sugary drinks a day had lower motility (cross-sectional) [tbody-chiu2014]; lead time extrapolated from sperm production [tbody-misell2006].

timing.debate: Glucose swings drove oxidative stress in clamp and type 2 diabetes studies [tbody-ceriello2008, tbody-monnier2006] but not in a type 1 diabetes CGM study [tbody-wentholt2008].

timing.summary: Each session raises muscle protein synthesis for about two days; strength rises in the first weeks mainly through the nervous system and muscle growth takes over after 3-5 weeks and continues for months. Muscle size is lost over months off, but much of the strength and some cellular 'memory' remain.

onset.text: Muscle protein synthesis stayed raised 48 h after a bout [tbody-phillips1997]; early strength gains in the first 3-5 weeks are mainly neural [tbody-moritani1979].

full.text: Protein synthesis tracks hypertrophy from about week 3 once muscle damage subsides [tbody-damas2016]; gains continue over months of progressive training.

after_stopping.text: After 20 weeks off, muscle size was back to baseline but ~60% of the strength gain remained [tbody-psilander2019]; extra myonuclei persisted 16 weeks [tbody-cumming2024] and methylation changes 7 weeks [tbody-seaborne2018].

frequency.text: 2-3 sessions a week to build. Once built, one-third or even one-ninth of the dose (about 1 session a week) kept muscle in young adults for 32 weeks, but older adults needed more [tbody-bickel2011, tbody-spiering2021].

timing.debate: One study found previously trained muscle did not regrow faster [tbody-psilander2019], while others found persistent myonuclei and epigenetic marks that favour regrowth [tbody-cumming2024, tbody-seaborne2018].

timing.summary: Long sitting raises that day's post-meal glucose, and a week or two of very low activity cuts insulin sensitivity and fitness. Young people bounce back quickly, but in older prediabetic adults two weeks of normal activity were not enough to recover.

onset.text: Breaking up sitting lowered same-day post-meal glucose and insulin [tbody-dunstan2012]; short bed rest cut insulin-stimulated glucose disposal 42% [tbody-dirks2020].

full.text: Two weeks at ~1,350 steps/day lowered insulin sensitivity 17% and VO2max 7% [tbody-kroghmadsen2010].

after_stopping.text: In trained young people one exercise bout almost restored glucose responses after 10 inactive days [tbody-heath1983]; in prediabetic older adults glycaemic control and muscle protein synthesis had not recovered after 2 weeks of normal activity [tbody-mcglory2018].

frequency.text: Short walking breaks every 20-30 min [tbody-dunstan2012].

timing.debate: Bed-rest insulin resistance occurred without a rise in mitochondrial H2O2 or oxidative markers [tbody-dirks2020], so the oxidative-stress route for sitting harms is unproven; no substantive published debate on timing found.

timing.summary: Living out of step with the body clock raises blood pressure and inflammation within three days, and these lab changes normalise within about nine days of regular sleep. Years of rotating night shifts carry a heart-disease risk that fades only gradually over years after quitting.

onset.text: Three days of 12-h misalignment raised 24-h blood pressure and IL-6, CRP and TNF-alpha by 3-29% [tbody-morris2016]; 10 days of a 28-h day raised glucose and blood pressure [tbody-scheer2009].

full.text: Coronary risk rose with years of rotating night shifts [tbody-vetter2016].

after_stopping.text: Lab metabolic changes normalised within 9 days of recovery sleep and re-entrainment [tbody-buxton2012]; the excess coronary risk waned with longer time since quitting shift work over years [tbody-vetter2016].

frequency.text: Limit consecutive nights and total years of rotating nights where possible.

egg.text: Shift work is linked to menstrual disruption [tbody-stocker2014]; the lead time is extrapolated from follicle growth (~85 days) [tbody-gougeon1986].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

timing.summary: One sleepless night lowers blood glutathione, and a week of short sleep raises CRP, worsens glucose tolerance and lowers testosterone. Two or three long nights reverse some of this, but weekend catch-up does not protect metabolism if weekday restriction continues.

onset.text: One night without sleep lowered plasma glutathione [tbody-trivedi2017]; 6-10 nights of short sleep raised CRP and worsened glucose tolerance [tbody-meierewert2004, tbody-spiegel1999]; one week of 5 h nights lowered testosterone [tbody-leproult2011].

full.text: Six weeks of 1.5 h less sleep increased endothelial oxidative stress [tbody-shah2023].

after_stopping.text: IL-6 and sleepiness normalised after 2 recovery nights but attention did not [tbody-pejovic2013]; glucose tolerance normalised after 6 recovery nights [tbody-spiegel1999]; weekend recovery did not prevent loss of insulin sensitivity when restriction resumed [tbody-depner2019].

frequency.text: Sleep has to be regular; catching up at weekends is not a substitute [tbody-depner2019].

sperm.late_start: Testosterone responds within a week of sleep change [tbody-leproult2011], but sperm already in production would not benefit fully.
sperm.text: Short or long sleep was linked to lower sperm counts (cross-sectional) [tbody-coleman2026]; lead time extrapolated from sperm production [tbody-misell2006].

egg.text: Short sleep and trouble sleeping were linked to lower fecundability [tbody-willis2019]; lead time extrapolated from follicle growth [tbody-gougeon1986].

timing.debate: Extended weekend sleep reversed IL-6 and sleepiness after a week of mild restriction [tbody-pejovic2013], but in a repeating weekday-restriction pattern weekend recovery did not protect insulin sensitivity [tbody-depner2019].

timing.summary: Effective CPAP lowers blood pressure and improves blood vessel function within weeks, and lowered an oxidative marker after 12 weeks in one trial but not after 8 weeks in a larger one. Stopping CPAP brings apnoea back within days and blood pressure up within two weeks.

onset.text: Blood-pressure and endothelial benefits are evident within 2 weeks (inferred from withdrawal) [tbody-kohler2011].

full.text: Plasma 8-isoprostane fell after 12 weeks of CPAP versus sham [tbody-alonsofernandez2009]; total antioxidant capacity rose across therapy durations [tbody-hosseini2023].

after_stopping.text: OSA returned within days and morning blood pressure rose +8.5/6.9 mmHg within 2 weeks [tbody-kohler2011], but blood oxidative markers did not rise in 2 weeks [tbody-stradling2015].

frequency.text: Nightly use; the benefit is lost within days of stopping [tbody-kohler2011].

timing.debate: CPAP lowered 8-isoprostane at 12 weeks [tbody-alonsofernandez2009] and raised antioxidant capacity in a meta-analysis [tbody-hosseini2023], but a 153-person sham-controlled trial found no change in F2-isoprostanes after 2 months [tbody-pazymar2016] and withdrawal did not raise oxidative markers [tbody-stradling2015].

timing.summary: A daily eating window changes glucose within days and gives about 3% weight loss over two months, mostly by cutting calories. Over a year it adds little beyond the calorie deficit, and benefits would fade as weight returns.

onset.text: Four days of eating 8 am-2 pm lowered 24-h glucose [tbody-jamshed2019].

full.text: Five weeks of early 6-h eating improved insulin sensitivity and oxidative stress [tbody-sutton2018]; 8 weeks of 4-6 h windows cut weight ~3% [tbody-cienfuegos2020]; 12 months gave no significant extra weight loss over calorie restriction alone [tbody-liu2022].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Studied daily; no trial compared fewer days per week.

timing.debate: Weight-stable early TRE improved insulin sensitivity [tbody-sutton2018], but intended-isocaloric TRE did not [tbody-peters2025] and calorie-matched TRE added no significant benefit over 12 months [tbody-liu2022].

timing.summary: Under-fuelling hard training disrupts the reproductive hormone pulse within five days, and menstrual disturbance follows. Eating about 330 kcal a day more restored cycles in most women who recovered within three to six months.

onset.text: LH pulsatility was disrupted within 5 days once energy availability fell below 30 kcal/kg lean mass per day [tbody-loucks2003].

full.text: Not measured prospectively; cycle disturbance develops over months of low energy availability [tbody-mountjoy2023].

after_stopping.text: With ~330 kcal/day more food, 67% of recoveries happened within 3 months and 78% within 6 months, in a 12-month trial [tbody-desouza2021].

frequency.text: Lean women trying to conceive: vigorous exercise of 5+ h/week was linked to lower fecundability [tbody-wise2012]; energy intake must match training every day [tbody-mountjoy2023].

egg.late_start: Eating more and cutting volume 2-4 weeks before may restore LH pulses within days [tbody-loucks2003], but regular ovulation usually needs months [tbody-desouza2021].
egg.text: Restoring energy balance acts on the hypothalamic signal for follicle growth; since most menstrual recoveries took up to 6 months [tbody-desouza2021] and the follicle grows ~85 days [tbody-gougeon1986], start early.

timing.debate: Very active women had more fertility problems [tbody-gudmundsdottir2009, tbody-wise2012], yet the most intensely active women were not more often childless at follow-up [tbody-gudmundsdottir2009], suggesting the harm is reversible.
